title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 14)
summary: Part 14 of NH's Meditations reading, recorded in the rain. He covers seeking approval from people you dislike, fame versus posterity, refusing self-imposed limits, avoiding wrongdoers without hatred, changing your mind when shown the truth while keeping an intellectual backbone, and correcting others patiently instead of with anger. He admits he tends to berate beginners and needs to work on it.
claims: Seeking praise from contemporaries you dislike is illogical; seek the appreciation of like-minded people to stay true to yourself
Fame is toxic and fleeting; posterity happens after death when you can't see it
He cares more about being worthy of his ancestors' praise, e.g. his great-grandfather, than of neighbours or future people
Never call something impossible; ask under what conditions it is possible. The only person who can limit you is yourself
Saying something is impossible is often an excuse to avoid trying and failing; a loser's mindset
Bad actors survive because people are too lenient; correcting them helps them integrate society
Avoid people who hurt you, but logically, without hatred; resentment lets them live in your head
Stoicism isn't rigidity; it is a guideline that follows truth, and truth only liberates
His first reaction to contradiction is emotional; after stepping back he can assess it and has changed things on the channel after viewer feedback
If you don't look back after a year or two and think you were an idiot, you are stagnating
Stupidity is refusing to know or change your mind, not ignorance
Avoid relativism: keep an intellectual backbone and strong opinions, open to change only through correct arguments; don't be a fence-sitter
Don't be swayed by objects, by irrational people who only look logical, or by people who abandoned reason
Anger at someone's mistakes teaches them not to try again; correct them patiently with evidence
He tends to berate beginners because a kick in the butt got him started, but it can push people away from lifting and he needs to work on it
On the channel he gives keys but doesn't open doors; people must work things out themselves
Remember where you came from and welcome newcomers to lifting with open arms
